segments.text: The everyday "how are you?" needs one more k- question word — how. And, being an adjective-like word, it too carries gender.
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) क (ka) + सा (sā) becomes कसा kasā; क + शी (śī) becomes कशी kaśī; क + सं (saṁ) becomes कसं kasaṁ.

कसा (kasā, "how") belongs to the same k- question family as kāy (what), koṇ (who), kuṭhe (where) — all from PIE kʷo-, the root behind English how (yes, how is a wh- word that lost its w-spelling) and Latin quo-modo ("in what way," which became Spanish cómo).

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "how" agrees with who you ask

segments.text: Because it describes the person's state, how takes their gender:
कसा (kasā) — asking a man.
कशी (kaśī) — asking a woman.
कसं (kasaṁ) — asking about a neuter thing.
So "how are you?" changes shape with whom you address — you will see this in the next lesson.

lessons.title: तुम्ही कसे आहात? (tumhī kase āhāt?) — "how are you?"

segments.text: The full courteous "how are you?" — assembled from words you already hold.
तुम्ही (tumhī, respectful "you") + कसे (kase, "how," plural-agreeing).
आहात (āhāt, "are," respectful) becomes तुम्ही कसे आहात? — "you how are?", verb last.
Two agreements are at work:
Because तुम्ही is grammatically plural, "how" appears as कसे (kase, the plural form of kasā), and the copula as आहात (āhāt).
To a single male friend: तू कसा आहेस? (tū kasā āhes?); to a female friend: तू कशी आहेस? (tū kaśī āhes?).
The respectful tumhī … āhāt is the safe default with anyone new. The gendered kasā/kaśī only appears in the familiar tū form — one more place Marathi's three genders surface in ordinary speech.

segments.text: To answer "how are you?", you need to say I. In Marathi that is a single bright syllable: मी (mī).
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) मी = म (ma) + the long-ī stroke ी becomes mī.

मी (mī, "I") descends from Sanskrit अहम् (aham, "I"), which wore down over centuries to the short mī. That aham comes from PIE h₁eǵ(H)om — the ancestor of Latin ego and English I. And notice its family tie to last chapter's माझं (mājhaṁ, "my"): the same first-person m- thread runs through "I" and "my," just as English pairs I with me/my.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "I am" is mī āhe

segments.text: Pair मी with the copula आहे: मी आहे (mī āhe, "I am"). To answer that you are well, reach back to Chapter 2's बरं (baraṁ, "fine") in its gendered form: मी बरा आहे (mī barā āhe, a man) / मी बरी आहे (mī barī āhe, a woman) — "I am fine."

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "mī" — I; then "mī āhe" — I am]

segments.text: What links mī ("I") and mājhaṁ ("my")? (The shared first-person m- root — as English links I with me/my.)

lessons.title: मी बरा आहे (mī barā āhe) — "I'm well, thank you"
lessons.gloss: I'm well, thank you (mī barā āhe)

segments.text: The answer to "how are you?" — and it reuses a word you already banked in Chapter 2.
मी (mī, I) + बरा (barā, "well/fine") + आहे (āhe, am) becomes मी बरा आहे — "I am well." Add thanks: मी बरा आहे, धन्यवाद (mī barā āhe, dhanyavād).
Back in Chapter 2 you met बरं (baraṁ) standing alone as "okay/fine" — its neuter form. When it describes you, it takes your gender:
बरा (barā) — a man is well.
बरी (barī) — a woman is well.
बरं (baraṁ) — the bare "okay" (neuter).

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the copula changes with the subject

segments.text: You now have three forms of āhe in play: मी आहे (mī āhe, I am), तू आहेस (tū āhes, you are, familiar), तुम्ही आहात (tumhī āhāt, you are, respectful). One verb, reshaped for each person — Marathi marks who on the verb itself.

segments.instruction: "mī barā āhe, dhanyavād" (man) / "mī barī āhe, dhanyavād" (woman)

lessons.title: काही हरकत नाही (kāhī harkat nāhī) — "no problem / you're welcome"
lessons.gloss: no problem / you're welcome (kāhī harkat nāhī)

segments.text: When someone thanks you, Marathi's easy reply is not "you're welcome" but "there's no objection at all."
काही (kāhī, "any") + हरकत (harkat, "objection, trouble") + नाही (nāhī, "not/none") becomes "any objection there-is-not" ≈ "no problem at all."
Two threads meet here:
नाही (nāhī, "not") is Chapter 2's "no," on the ancient negative na- — PIE ne, the root of English no, not, none and Latin nōn.

हरकत (harkat, "objection, hindrance") is a Perso-Arabic loan (from Arabic ḥarakah), one of the many words Marathi absorbed over centuries of contact with Persian-speaking rulers and traders — the same trade-and-court layer that colours all the languages of the Deccan.
So the reply blends an Indo-European negative with an Arabic noun — a small map of Marathi's history in three words.
Where English "thank you / you're welcome" trades politeness tokens, Marathi waves the thanks away: don't mention it, there was no trouble. The same gesture, a different picture.

segments.text: कसा / कशी / कसं (kasā/kaśī/kasaṁ) — how; the k- question family, gender-agreeing.
मी (mī) — I; Sanskrit aham becomes Latin ego, English I.
बरा / बरी / बरं (barā/barī/baraṁ) — well/fine, now gendered.
काही हरकत नाही (kāhī harkat nāhī) — no problem; nāhī from PIE ne, harkat from Arabic.
Copula forms: मी आहे / तू आहेस / तुम्ही आहात (mī āhe / tū āhes / tumhī āhāt) — one verb, reshaped per person.
